steps.prompt: Why train a robot in a video game first?
steps.sub: Before a real robot ever moves, we teach it inside a simulator — a physics-accurate video game of itself. By the end you'll know what a digital twin is, the three reasons we train in sim first, and the one catch when we cross back to reality.

steps.prompt: First instinct — a robotics team wants a robot dog to learn to walk. What do they do FIRST?

options.t: Build the real dog and let it fall over on concrete a few thousand times until it learns.
Build a physics-accurate virtual copy of the dog and let it try to walk inside a simulator.
Write the exact walking motion by hand, joint by joint, and hope it works.

steps.why: Learning to walk takes thousands of clumsy, falling-over attempts. On a real robot each fall risks cracked joints and burned-out motors — slow and expensive. In a simulator the dog can fall ten thousand times for free, then we move the learned skill to the real robot. Hand-writing every joint angle almost never produces natural movement.
hints: Learning a motor skill means failing many, many times. Where is failing cheap and safe?
Real hardware breaks when it falls. A virtual copy doesn't.

steps.prompt: Three reasons we train in simulation first.
steps.sub: Tap each card. These three are the whole pitch for sim.

cards.b: A robot can fall, crash, or flail with zero broken hardware and no one hurt. Mistakes cost nothing.
Sim can run faster than real time, and a GPU runs thousands of copies at once — years of practice in hours.
No motors to replace, no lab to rent, no human to supervise each try. Failure is free, so you can fail a lot.

steps.sub: Tap each card. This is the one term to remember from this lesson.

cards.b: A digital twin is a virtual version of the real robot AND its environment — built to behave like the real thing.
It has the robot's real mass, joint limits, friction, and gravity — so what it learns transfers to reality.
You train the robot's skill in the twin, watch it, break it, fix it — all before touching real hardware.

steps.prompt: Which of these is a true digital twin of a warehouse robot — not just a cartoon of one?
steps.sub: Pick the one built to behave like the real robot.

options.t: A pretty 3D drawing of the robot that looks right but has no weight, no gravity, no friction.
A model with the robot's real mass, motor limits, wheel friction, and the shelves it must dodge — all under simulated gravity.
A photo of the robot on the company website.

steps.why: A digital twin isn't about looking right — it's about behaving right. It needs the real physics (mass, friction, joint limits, gravity) and the real surroundings, so a skill learned in the twin actually works on the metal robot. A drawing or photo has no physics, so nothing learned on it would transfer.
hints: A twin has to BEHAVE like the real robot, not just look like it.
Which option mentions mass, friction, and gravity — the things that make movement realistic?

steps.prompt: Sort each task: is simulation a great fit, or a poor fit?
steps.sub: Tap an item, then tap a bin.

items.t: Letting a robot arm try 50,000 grasps to learn picking
Teaching a drone to recover from a stall without crashing real drones
Final sign-off that the robot is safe to ship to a customer's factory
Running 4,000 robot copies in parallel to learn walking overnight
Measuring the exact smell and dust of the real warehouse floor

hints: Sim shines when you need MANY cheap, safe, repeatable tries.
Sim is weak when you need the messy, exact truth of the real world — final safety sign-off, real dust and wear.

steps.prompt: Tap the stages of the sim-to-real idea in order.
steps.sub: This is the journey from virtual practice to a working real robot.
chips: Deploy the learned skill onto the real robot
Build a digital twin of the robot + its world
Train the skill in the simulator (thousands of tries)
hints: You can't train inside a twin you haven't built yet.
Build it → practice in it → then cross over to the real robot.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check all at once.

statements.t: Because sim runs many robot copies at once on a GPU, it can pack years of practice into a few hours.
statements.why: Yes — running thousands of parallel copies is the superpower of GPU simulation. That parallelism is exactly why sim is so much faster than one real robot trying one thing at a time.

statements.t: A skill learned in simulation always works perfectly on the real robot, with no surprises.
statements.why: No — the sim is never a perfect copy of reality (slightly off friction, wear, sensor noise). That difference is the 'reality gap', and it's the catch we manage when crossing from sim to real.

statements.t: A digital twin needs to match the real robot's physics, not just its looks.
statements.why: Right — looks don't transfer, physics does. The twin needs real mass, friction, and joint limits so the learned skill carries over to hardware.

statements.t: Training on the real robot first is the cheap, safe way to start.
statements.why: No — real hardware is the expensive, risky place to fail. We fail cheaply in sim first, then move the polished skill to the real robot.

hints: Think about why teams bother with sim at all: safe, fast, cheap.
Is the simulator a PERFECT copy of reality, or a very close one?

steps.sub: Not graded. We use this to ground the rest of the course in something you actually care about.
